protocol.name: spatiand_xr_v1

description.summary: stereoscopic and head-tracked surfaces

protocol.description:
This is a protocol about applications, not about video. Any application may want to be stereoscopic -- a modelling tool, a map, a game, a terminal with depth to it -- and the compositor's job is to let it appear the way it means to appear, whatever it draws. A media player is only the first client.
Three things a Wayland client needs in order to draw for a head, and cannot get any other way:
1. a way to say how the two eyes' views are packed into its buffer, 2. a way to say what the surface *is* in the world -- a panel, something pinned to the view, a pair of eye views, or the sky itself, 3. the head and eye poses, before it renders.
Everything else it already has. A wl_buffer is the swapchain, a frame callback is the frame loop, a wl_surface is the layer. This protocol deliberately adds nothing that Wayland already carries.
HYBRID CLIENTS
A client that binds nothing here is an ordinary window, and an ordinary window is what it stays. Every request below is opt-in and every one has a defined meaning on a compositor that is showing the surface flat. The intended shape is one application that runs on a normal desktop, runs as a flat window here, and turns itself stereoscopic or immersive when it finds this global -- not three applications, and not a mode switch.
COORDINATES
This protocol's frame is **OpenXR's**, not the compositor's: +X right, +Y up, -Z forward, right-handed, metres, and quaternions in (x, y, z, w) order. The compositor's own frame is different and is not exposed here.
That is a deliberate choice at the boundary. It makes an OpenXR adapter a memcpy rather than a translation layer, and it means every convention a VR developer already has in their fingers is the right one. The structures in the pose channel are field-compatible with XrPosef and XrFovf for the same reason.
UNITS ON THE WIRE
Wayland has no floating point. The rarely-sent values here are signed integers in micro-units: micrometres for distance, microradians for angle. The per-frame values are not on the wire at all -- see the pose channel.

interface.name: spatiand_xr_v1

description.summary: stereoscopic and head-tracked surfaces

interface.description: The factory. Binding it says nothing and changes nothing.

request.name: destroy

description.summary: destroy the factory

request.description: Objects already created stay valid.

request.name: get_xr_surface

description.summary: extend a surface with stereo and layer state

request.description: One per wl_surface for its lifetime. Requesting a second is a protocol error, because two objects setting the layout of one surface have no defined resolution.

request.name: get_pose_channel

description.summary: ask for the shared-memory pose channel

request.description: See spatiand_xr_pose_channel_v1. A client that only shows pre-packed stereo -- a side-by-side film, say -- does not need this and should not ask for it: it is the compositor's head tracking, and asking for it while not using it is the difference between a player and a headset application.

request.name: ask_system

description.summary: the system's own applications, where a client cannot ask itself

request.description:
What only the room can ask of the system it runs on, for a client that cannot: on Android only the app's own Java may ask the PackageManager which applications open a kind of file, or start one with it, and Spatiand's applications are native programs inside it. Elsewhere a client asks the system itself (a desktop entry, Launch Services) and the room answers `{"error": ...}`.
One JSON object; the answer, JSON, is written into `answer`, which the room then closes:
- `{"do": "openers", "path": p, "type": mime}`: the applications that open that file, `{"apps": [{"id", "name", "default", "icon"}]}`, `icon` a PNG file the client may read, the system's own choice first. - `{"do": "all_openers", "type": mime}`: every application that opens files at all, for a choice of any. - `{"do": "open_with", "id": app, "path": p, "type": mime}`: open the file with that application, in the room, as any of the system's own applications is opened there; `{"ok": true}` once it is on its way.
And one the room answers itself, on every system:
- `{"do": "open_link", "url": u, "profile": id}`: open that address of the web in SpatiMesh -- started if it is not running, else handed to the one that is. `profile`, where given, is one of SpatiMesh's profiles as its folder in the shared data is named (its folder in `apps/spatimesh/profiles`); without it SpatiMesh opens the profile it would open itself. A profile with a lock is opened behind its lock: SpatiMesh asks for it in its own window, as for a new window of that profile, and opens nothing if it is refused. `{"ok": true}` once it is on its way. - `{"do": "open_embedded", "token": t, "url": u, "profile": id}` (since 13): open that address -- of the web, or `file:` for a file of the wearer's -- in SpatiMesh as the inside of a place in the asker's own window, the place whose `token` this is (spatiand_xr_embed_v1): no tabs, no address bar, no frame. `profile` as for `open_link`. `{"ok": true}` once it is on its way; the place says `attached` when it has it.
An answer of `{"error": "..."}` says what went wrong in words fit to show.

event.name: display_mode

description.summary: whether the wearer is being shown one picture or two

event.description:
Sent once when the global is bound, and again whenever it changes -- the glasses unplugged from a Mac, which then shows its windows on its own screen; a headset that has only just gone into its two-eye mode.
Nothing a client has claimed is taken away by it: an eye layout is still honoured in "flat", by showing one eye's half to both. It is for the client that has a choice -- one that can draw a model once or twice, or that would rather show a film's left eye at full sharpness than have it halved -- to make it at the moment it matters and not from a guess. A flat window that binds this and ignores the event is an ordinary window and stays one.

event.name: hands

description.summary: the wearer's hands did something

event.description:
A pad touched or moved, a mouse moved, a button, a scroll, a key: whatever wakes the room's own idle clock (set_idle_fade), and **never the head**. Sent at most a few times a second, whatever the surface under the pointer.
A pointer's motion over a surface is not this: the pointer is cast from the head, so it sweeps across surfaces whenever the wearer looks about. A client fading controls of its own -- drawn into its own picture, where set_idle_fade cannot reach -- wakes them on this and on a press, and not on motion.

entry.name: flat
entry.summary: one picture, the same for both eyes or on a screen

entry.name: stereo
entry.summary: each eye is drawn its own picture

interface.name: spatiand_xr_surface_v1

description.summary: how a surface is drawn for two eyes

interface.description: All state here is double-buffered: it takes effect on the next wl_surface.commit, like everything else about a surface. Changing layout between frames is expected and costs nothing -- a player showing a side-by-side film with a flat menu over it changes it twice a second.

request.name: destroy

description.summary: stop treating this surface specially

request.description: The surface reverts to mono, layer "window", on the next commit.

request.name: set_eye_layout

description.summary: how the two eyes are packed into the buffer

request.description:
With "mono" both eyes are shown the same pixels; this is the default and is what a surface that never calls this does.
For the split layouts the two eyes sample opposite halves of the SAME buffer while the surface keeps ONE position in the world. Full-width and half-width side-by-side are not distinguished, because they are not different: each eye is given its half stretched across the surface, and only the sharpness differs. Send the source as it is.

entry.name: mono
entry.summary: both eyes see the whole buffer

entry.name: side_by_side
entry.summary: left eye in the left half

entry.name: top_bottom
entry.summary: left eye in the top half

request.name: set_eye_swapped

description.summary: the halves are the other way round

request.description: Some sources are packed right-eye-first and nothing in the file says so. A viewer needs a control for that which does not mean re-encoding.

request.name: set_layer

description.summary: what this surface is in the world

request.description:
See the layer enum. A compositor that cannot honour a layer -- the sky is already taken, say -- answers with layer_refused and keeps drawing the surface as a window, which is always a valid thing to be.
THERE IS NO "GRANTED" EVENT, AND SILENCE IS THE YES. A layer is honoured without comment and refused out loud, so a client can never lay itself out for something it is not getting. What that means in practice: send set_layer, then wl_display.sync, and if no layer_refused arrived before the sync callback, the layer is yours. Do not wait for anything else; nothing else is coming.

entry.name: window

description.summary: an ordinary panel in the room

entry.description: The default. Moved and resized by the wearer, stays where it is put. The OpenXR quad layer is this.

entry.name: head_locked

description.summary: a panel that follows the view

entry.description: Keeps its angular size and position relative to the head. For content that must stay in front of you, and for a client doing its own head tracking -- a nested runtime, say -- where the compositor moving the surface as well would apply tracking twice.

entry.name: projection

description.summary: the client has rendered the two eye views itself

entry.description: The buffer is what the eyes should see, drawn by the client from the poses in the pose channel, and is presented filling the view rather than as a panel in it. Requires an eye layout other than mono. The OpenXR projection layer is this.

entry.name: equirect_180

description.summary: the client is the sky, front hemisphere

entry.description:
Equirectangular, covering 180 degrees of longitude in front of the wearer. Behind them there is no image and the compositor says so rather than smearing the edge.
"In front of the wearer" is where they were facing when the layer was claimed, and the image then stays put. This matters far more here than for equirect_360, where turning the wrong way merely shows a different part of the picture rather than the absence of one.

description.summary: the client is the sky, all of it

request.name: set_yaw_offset

description.summary: turn an immersive image about the vertical axis

request.description:
Microradians, positive to the left. Only meaningful for the equirect layers, where it brings the interesting part of a panorama round to face the wearer's forward. Ignored otherwise.
This is a statement about the IMAGE, not about where the image goes. An immersive layer already arrives centred on the wearer -- the compositor notes which way they are facing when the layer is claimed, exactly as it does when placing a new window, and the image stays there afterwards however they turn. So a client wanting its content in front of the person watching should send nothing at all; this is for the separate case of a panorama whose interesting part is not at its centre.
Do not compensate for head position here. A client that reads the pose channel and sends the negated heading will find its two rotations adding up against a compositor that is already doing it.

event.name: layer_refused

description.summary: the compositor will not do that

event.description: The surface keeps whatever layer it had. Carries the layer that was asked for, so a client that asked for two things knows which failed, and a human-readable reason which is for a log and not for a user.

event.name: layer_lost

description.summary: an exclusive layer has been taken away

event.description: Sent when the wearer or another client takes back something only one surface can have -- the sky. The surface is a window again from the next frame. A client that crashes cannot leave the wearer inside a frozen image, because the same thing happens when its surface dies.

request.name: set_idle_fade

description.summary: let the compositor fade this surface out when unattended

request.description:
For a surface that should get out of the way -- a transport bar over a film, a toolbar over a model -- and come back when the wearer wants it.
The compositor owns the timer, the threshold and the animation, and that is the point of putting it here rather than leaving it to the client. A client cannot do this correctly even in principle: pointer motion is delivered only to the surface under the ray, so a surface that has faded out cannot see the wearer reaching for it, and has no way to know it should come back. The compositor sees every pointer sample and every head movement, whatever they are pointed at.
While faded the surface is STILL THE INPUT TARGET, at every alpha including zero. Pressing where an invisible transport bar is will hit it -- but the same motion has already brought it back, so in practice the wearer sees it before they press it.
The surface keeps rendering; nothing about its buffers, frame callbacks or size changes, and a client need not know whether it is currently faded. It is a compositor-side dimmer on an otherwise ordinary window.
Off by default. This is double-buffered like everything else here.

request.name: set_idle_after

description.summary: how long unattended is long enough

request.description:
Milliseconds of the wearer doing nothing before this surface starts to fade. Zero means the compositor's own idea, which is also what a surface that never calls this gets.
The right answer is a property of what the surface IS, not of the session: a toolbar over a model wants to stay while you think, and a transport bar over a film wants to be gone the moment you stop touching it. No single number serves both, which is why this is here rather than being something the compositor decides for everybody.
Only the threshold is yours. The animation, and what counts as the wearer doing something, stay the compositor's — those are properties of the room and of the input hardware, and a client cannot see either.
The compositor may clamp this. Below about a second the ramps are longer than the wait, so the surface never reaches full brightness before starting back down, and what a client asking for 200 ms actually gets is a flicker. Ask for what you mean and expect something sensible.
No effect without set_idle_fade.

request.name: set_resize_anchor

description.summary: which edge stays put when this surface changes shape

request.description:
A surface has one position in the room and its height follows from its buffer's aspect, so committing a shorter buffer makes it shrink about its middle. For a window becoming a transport bar -- same width, a fifth the height -- that leaves the bar floating in the centre of the view with film above it AND below it, where what was wanted was the bar sitting where the bottom of the window used to be.
This says which edge means something. "bottom" keeps the bottom edge where it was and takes the height off the top, "top" the other way round, and "centre" is the old behaviour and the default.
Deliberately an anchor rather than a way to move yourself. A client that can set its own position will set its own position, and then placement stops being one thing the compositor decides -- the wearer moves a window and the application puts it back. An anchor states the intent and leaves the geometry here.
Applies to the surface's own content. The chrome around it is the compositor's business and may change thickness independently.

entry.name: centre
entry.summary: shrink about the middle; the default

entry.name: top
entry.summary: the top edge stays where it is

entry.name: bottom
entry.summary: the bottom edge stays where it is

request.name: set_cursor_drawn

description.summary: this surface draws the pointer itself

request.description:
While the pointer is over this surface, the compositor draws no reticle and no beam for it; the client draws its own.
The compositor knows which way the pointer points and nothing about how far away what it points at is. For a window that does not matter: the window is the depth. For a surface that is the room -- a projection layer, where one pixel is a table two metres off and the next is a mountain -- a reticle drawn at the room's depth is at the wrong depth almost everywhere, and seen double against whatever the wearer is actually aiming at. The client drew the room and knows the depth of every pixel of it, so the client draws the cursor.
Where the pointer is still arrives as ordinary pointer motion, in the surface's own coordinates. Only the drawing moves. Over any other surface, or over none, the compositor draws the pointer as it always does.
Off by default. Double-buffered like everything else here.

request.name: set_frame_pose

description.summary: the head this surface's picture was drawn for

request.description:
For a `projection` surface: where the head was pointing in the picture attached with the next commit -- the orientation the client rendered its eye views from, which is not where the head is by the time they are shown. Between reading the pose and the picture reaching the glass are the client's rendering and the compositor's own wait for the next display frame, and a picture drawn for one head and shown to another swims against the world when the head moves.
Told the difference, the compositor turns the picture by it before showing it, so the world stays where it is. Rotation only: a few centimetres of head movement in a few milliseconds is not what anyone sees, and what a rotation cannot fix a translation cannot be asked to.
The quaternion is the head's orientation in this protocol's frame (see COORDINATES), each component in millionths. A surface that never says is shown as though drawn for the head as it is now. Double-buffered, so the pose and the picture it belongs to arrive together.
`token` is a number the pose channel's slot carried when the client read it (its `reserved` field, which is otherwise zero), handed back so that a compositor that is only passing the picture on -- to a headset across a network, say -- can say which head it was drawn for without the two ends agreeing on a clock. Zero means none.

arg.name: token
arg.summary: the slot's reserved field, or zero

request.name: set_pinch_taken

description.summary: this surface zooms its own content when pinched

request.description:
Two fingers pinching or spreading over a window ordinarily make the window itself bigger or smaller. A surface that has something of its own to zoom -- a picture, a page -- says so with this, and is sent `pinch` instead while the pointer is over it; the window stays the size it is. Pinching on the window's title bar is the compositor's still.
Off by default. Double-buffered like everything else here.

request.name: set_see_through

description.summary: what this surface leaves clear is clear

request.description:
A window is drawn opaque whatever its buffer's alpha says: a client's own transparency would let the room through a terminal and make it unreadable. A surface whose content is a thing on nothing -- a picture shown whole, its shape not the window's -- asks with this for its alpha to be kept, so that where it draws nothing the room is seen.
Off by default. Double-buffered like everything else here.

request.name: set_sound_key

description.summary: which sound is this window's

request.description:
A client that hands its sound to the compositor itself -- rather than playing it where the compositor can see which process made it -- says with what name it hands it over, so that the sound is placed at this window and not at another window of the same application. Each window of a client may have a key of its own (two pages of a browser, three films in three windows of one player) or share one.
The name is the client's to choose and means nothing else. A window that never says is placed by its application id, as before.
Double-buffered like everything else here.

arg.name: key
arg.summary: the name its sound is handed over with

request.name: set_scroll_free

description.summary: this surface scrolls both ways at once

request.description:
A thumb on a pad scrolls one way at a time: what its first movements choose, and up or down far more readily than sideways, because a thumb meaning to read down a page drifts sideways as it goes. A surface whose content moves both ways under the hand -- a picture swiped to the next, a map or a zoomed picture panned -- says so with this, and is sent both axes as the thumb moves, from its first movement past where the contact settles; which way that is, if either, is the client's to decide.
Off by default. Double-buffered like everything else here.

enum.name: media_key

description.summary: a keyboard's keys for what is playing

enum.description: The keys a keyboard has for a player, whatever the system it is plugged into calls them. `play_pause` is the one key most keyboards have for both; `play` and `pause` are a keyboard's that has one for each.

request.name: set_media_keys

description.summary: this surface is playing something

request.description:
A surface that is playing something the wearer would pause, or go forward or back in -- a film, music -- says so while it is, and is sent a keyboard's media keys with `media_key`, wherever the keyboard is typing: they are not the focused window's keys, and are never sent as keys. Of several surfaces that say so, the one the keyboard is typing into has them, or else the newest of them.
When no surface says so, the play key starts SpatiReel if it is not running, and does nothing if it is; the other keys do nothing.
Off by default; to be turned off when nothing is playing any more. Double-buffered like everything else here.

event.name: pinch

description.summary: the wearer pinched over this surface

event.description: How much the fingers spread since the last `pinch`: a factor, in millionths, above a million for spreading (zoom in) and below for drawing together. Sent only to a surface that asked with `set_pinch_taken`, as the fingers move.

event.name: describe

description.summary: say what this surface shows, for the room's speech

event.description:
The room asks what this surface is about: dictation leans its spelling towards a terminal's commands and a page's words, and the assistant reads a window through this.
The client writes one JSON object into the file descriptor and closes it, soon -- the room waits a moment, and then does without. Every field is optional: "kind" (terminal, web, files, video, viewer, chat, text), "app", "title", "text" (what it shows, as text), "vocabulary" (an array of names and words likely to be said: file names, a page's headings), "directory", and "commands" (a terminal's last commands, the last one last). A client with nothing to say closes it at once.
This is the client's own account of itself, and may hold more than is on show: a whole page, a terminal's scroll-back. It is not what the wearer sees. The assistant's account of what the wearer sees is the room's own picture of the window as it is shown (spatiand_assist_v1, "seen": cropped to the part in view, at whatever zoom it is drawn); this text goes with it only when a request reaches past what is on screen ("the rest of the article", "the other window"), and is marked to the model as not on screen. A client need not, and should not, try to answer with only what is on show.

event.name: media_key

description.summary: a media key was pressed or let go

event.description: A keyboard's media key, for this surface because it said it is playing (`set_media_keys`). `pressed` is 1 as the key goes down and 0 as it comes up; a key held is not repeated, and what holding one means -- to keep going forward -- is the client's to do between the two.

request.name: get_embed

description.summary: a place in this window for another application's window

request.description: A rectangle of this surface's window in which the room shows another application's window -- a page of SpatiMesh's inside a viewer's own, say -- as part of this one: what a toolkit calls a web view, between two programs. See spatiand_xr_embed_v1. Asked of a toplevel's surface; a window may have several.

request.name: set_embedded

description.summary: this window is the inside of another's place

request.description:
This surface's toplevel is the inside of the place whose token this is (spatiand_xr_embed_v1.token), not a window of the room's: it has no place, title bar or buttons of its own, is not among the windows the wearer switches between, and is sized by the place (xdg_toplevel.configure with its rectangle's size, which the client should take as it comes and draw no frame or shadow round). It is shown in the other window, pointed at and typed into there, and goes where that window goes -- hidden, moved, pinned, faded and closed with it. Its sound is heard from that window.
Double-buffered: it takes effect on the next commit, which should be the first, before anything is drawn, so that the window never appears in the room on its own. A token that names no place, or a place that has a window already, leaves this an ordinary window, and the room says so in its log. An empty token is no place.

arg.name: token
arg.summary: the place's token, as it was given

request.name: post_to_host

description.summary: say something to the window this one is inside

request.description: For the window this surface's window is the inside of (`set_embedded`): sent on there as spatiand_xr_embed_v1.message. What is said is the two applications' own business -- usually one JSON object; the room only carries it, keeping the order. Not delivered, and dropped, when this window is not the inside of a place.

event.name: host_message

description.summary: the window this one is inside said something

event.description: spatiand_xr_embed_v1.send, from the window this surface's window is the inside of.

interface.name: spatiand_xr_embed_v1

description.summary: a place in a window for another application's window

interface.description:
Made with spatiand_xr_surface_v1.get_embed, on the window that keeps the place -- the host. The room sends `token` at once: the name of this place, which the window to go in it is given -- by `ask_system`'s `open_embedded` for SpatiMesh, or, for a program the host starts itself, in that program's environment as SPATIAND_EMBED_TOKEN -- and says with spatiand_xr_surface_v1.set_embedded. One window at a time is the inside of a place.
The inside is drawn in the host's window at the rectangle, over the host's own picture and its subsurfaces and under the host's menus; its own menus may hang out of the rectangle, as any menu may out of its window. The pointer over it is its own, in its own coordinates; a press in it gives it the keyboard, and a press elsewhere in the host's window gives the keyboard back to the host.
Destroying this object, or the host's window closing, asks the inside to close (xdg_toplevel.close) and forgets the token.

request.name: destroy

description.summary: take the place away

request.description: The window inside is asked to close.

request.name: set_rect

description.summary: where the place is in the host's surface

request.description:
In the host surface's own coordinates, as its pointer events are. The window inside is configured to the rectangle's size whenever it changes. A rectangle of no size hides the inside and keeps it.
Double-buffered with the host's surface: it takes effect on the host's next wl_surface.commit, so that a host laying itself out anew moves the place in the same frame as its own picture.

request.name: send

description.summary: say something to the window inside

request.name: focus

description.summary: give the keyboard to the window inside

request.description: As a press in it would, while the host's window has the keyboard: for a host that opens a page meant to be typed into at once.

event.name: token

description.summary: the place's name

event.description: Sent once, as the object is made. Unguessable, and good for as long as the object lives: a window that closed can be followed by another with the same token.

event.name: attached

description.summary: a window is inside

event.description: The window that said set_embedded with this place's token has committed it; from now it is drawn here.

event.name: detached

description.summary: the window inside has gone

event.description: Closed or ended; the place is empty and keeps its token.

description.summary: the window inside said something

interface.name: spatiand_assist_v1

description.summary: the room's assistant: what is in the room, and doing things in it

interface.description:
The assistant is one of Spatiand's own programs, and through this it sees the room as the wearer does and acts in it as the wearer would: which applications and windows there are, what a window shows (its own account of itself, or a picture of it), and the pointer and keyboard on a window, the room's settings, and its own figure in the room.
Offered to every client and **refused to all but one**: until a client has said the key the room gave the assistant when it started it (`SPATIAND_ASSIST_KEY`, a secret per session, handed to no other program), every question is answered with an error. A key in the environment is not one a shell in a terminal inherits: the room gives it to the assistant's own process alone.
Questions and actions are JSON (`{"do": "...", ...}`), small enough for one message; the answer is JSON written into the file descriptor that came with the question, which the room closes when it is done. An answer of `{"error": "..."}` says what went wrong in words fit to show.

request.name: destroy

description.summary: done with the room

request.description: The microphone, if it was being given, stops.

request.name: hello

description.summary: say the key

request.description: The key from the environment. Said once, first; a wrong one closes nothing but leaves every question refused.

request.name: ask

description.summary: a question or an action

request.description:
One JSON object; the answer is written into `answer` and it is closed.
`{"do": "seen"}` is what the wearer sees, made by the room the same way for every window, on every platform: the window they are looking at (the one in the middle of the view; else the focused one in view; else the one filling most of it; never the assistant's own), its picture as shown -- the part inside the field of view only, at the zoom it is drawn at -- with which part that is (`part`, `[u0, u1, v0, v1]` of the window from its top left), how much of the view it fills, and the other windows in view. `"window"` names another; `"view": true` adds the left eye's picture of the whole view as last drawn (`view_png`); `"picture": false` leaves the pictures out. A room with no head to look from (a flat room) answers with every window whole. `{"do": "target"}`, the window a request with none named acts on, is likewise the one looked at when the room knows where the wearer looks.
`{"do": "avatar", ...}` is the assistant's figure, laid over what was said of it before (a key left out stays as it was): `path` its file (a GLB or a VRM; none for the room's own robot), `visible`, `state` (what it is doing: idle, listening, checking, attentive, hearing, transcribing, thinking, pondering, working, talking, happy; `mood` for a room older than these), `wave: true` (a wave, each time it is said), `size` (0.5 to 3 times its usual height), `signs` (the lights over its head, shown unless false), `options` (`{"group": "option"}`: a node named `group=option` is shown only while it is the one chosen, and a group's first option until one is), `pose` (an animation held until another is asked for, or none -- or, for a figure with a person's skeleton, a pose of its own making: an object of its body's parts, each with where it points from the figure's own point of view, `{"left_upper_arm": "down, out, a little back", "head": "tilt left"}`, held over its animation), `move` with `moves` (an animation played once, each time `moves` counts up), `expression` (a face held: a VRM expression, or a morph target by its name), `colors` (`{"material": "#rrggbb"}`), `motions` (`{"name": file}`: motions made from words, played as its animations of those names) and `character` (who the figure is: `pixel`, or `pal:` and the pal's folder). An animation named after the state plays by itself, `idle` standing in for any the figure lacks. A figure's skeleton is posed by the room the same way on every platform (docs/spatipal-pals.md).
Where the figure stands is the room's: beside the assistant's own window while that is on show in the view and the place beside it is in sight, else in a corner of the view, drawn smaller there rather than further in. The wearer may press and drag it elsewhere -- remembered for each `character` -- and a double press puts it back.
Only the room and the assistant use this interface: a copy of this file in a client (Chromium's) needs no change for what is added here, and is brought up to date with that client's next monthly build.

request.name: listen

description.summary: the microphone, while the assistant listens

request.description: The room writes the microphone into `fd` -- 16 kHz, mono, 16-bit little endian -- until either end closes it or `listen` is asked again. One microphone serves the whole room: dictation and the assistant share it.

event.name: happened

description.summary: something the assistant may want to know

event.description: JSON: `{"focus": window}` when the focus moves, `{"wake": true}` when the wearer asks for the assistant by a control (the mic key held, say).

interface.name: spatiand_xr_pose_channel_v1

description.summary: head and eye poses, in shared memory

interface.description:
Poses are NOT sent as events, and that is the central decision in this protocol.
A head-tracked client has to know where the head is at the last possible moment before it renders -- that is what makes the world stay still. An event carrying the pose is already stale when it arrives: it costs a round trip, it arrives when the compositor got round to sending it rather than when the client needs it, and it cannot be re-read a millisecond later without another round trip.
So the compositor writes poses into a small ring in shared memory and hands over a read-only file descriptor. The client maps it once and reads the newest sample whenever it likes, including immediately before submitting a frame. No round trips, no per-frame protocol traffic, and late-latching becomes a memory read.
The ring also carries a short history, so a client can interpolate to an arbitrary time -- which is exactly what an OpenXR adapter needs to answer xrLocateViews for a predicted display time.
MEMORY FORMAT
Little-endian, naturally aligned, and stable for the life of this interface version. All floats are IEEE-754 binary32. Times are CLOCK_MONOTONIC nanoseconds, the same clock a frame callback's time comes from.
struct spatiand_xr_channel { // offset 0 uint32_t version; // 1 uint32_t slot_count; // power of two uint32_t slot_stride; // bytes uint32_t slots_offset; // bytes from the start uint64_t write_index; // total slots ever written uint64_t _reserved; };
struct spatiand_xr_slot { // slots_offset + (i * slot_stride) uint64_t seq; // odd while being written int64_t sample_ns; // when this pose was measured int64_t predicted_ns; // when a frame submitted now is expected to be shown int64_t _reserved; float head_orientation[4]; // x, y, z, w -- XrQuaternionf float head_position[3]; // metres -- XrVector3f float _pad0; struct { float orientation[4]; // x, y, z, w float position[3]; // metres, relative to the tracking origin float _pad; float fov[4]; // angleLeft, angleRight, angleUp, angleDown // radians, signed -- XrFovf exactly } eye[2]; // 0 = left };
READING IT
Read `write_index`, take slot `(write_index - 1) modulo slot_count` (the count is a power of two, so this is a mask), read `seq`, read the body, read `seq` again. If either `seq` read is odd or the two differ, the writer was in that slot: step back one slot or try again. This is an ordinary seqlock and it never blocks the compositor.
The compositor writes at its own rate, which is the display rate. A client that reads faster will see repeats; one that reads slower will miss samples. Neither is an error.

request.name: destroy

description.summary: stop receiving poses

request.description: The mapping stays valid until the client unmaps it, but stops being updated.

event.name: channel

description.summary: here is the shared memory

event.description: Sent once, immediately. The descriptor is read-only and sealed; map it with MAP_SHARED and PROT_READ.

event.name: render_size

description.summary: the size the viewer wants each eye drawn at

event.description:
Sent when a viewer that is not on this machine -- a headset across a network, being streamed to -- has a size for each eye that is not the one the client would pick for itself, and again whenever it changes. A client that renders to its own idea of "an eye" is stretched to fit, which on a stream is a picture that has been resampled twice for nothing.
A compositor that drives the display directly has no such preference and never sends this. Dimensions are one eye's, in pixels; the client chooses its layout and multiplies them itself.

event.name: unavailable

description.summary: there are no poses to give

event.description: Sent instead of `channel` when the session has no head tracking at all -- no headset plugged in, or a nested session on a desktop. A client should carry on as a flat window rather than wait. It is not an error and the object stays alive; `channel` may arrive later if a headset appears.
